blocks.html: How do PIP and WID measure income inequality?

slides.notes:
- PIP is survey-based: built from household income surveys where they exist and consumption-expenditure surveys otherwise.
- Which one you get depends on the country. High-income countries mostly report income after taxes and benefits; most low- and middle-income countries report consumption. That mixture is a comparability issue we come back to.
- They do some transformations, e.g. everything is standardised to per capita, in 2021 international dollars.
- Availability: not all countries do surveys every year, - > chart
- A big strength is its coverage

[Figma node 6:17]

blocks.html:
PIP — overview
PIP “survey data”
Income survey
Consumption expenditure survey
Transformations:
Per capita
LCUs to int.-$
Bottom coding
add diagram of reference year we pick (line) and availability of surveys for some countries

slides.notes:
- PIP doesn't measure the same thing everywhere. For richer countries it mostly uses income after taxes and benefits; for most low- and middle-income countries it uses consumption, because that's what their surveys collect.
- Income and consumption are closely related but not the same, and the gap between them changes along the distribution.
- At the bottom, consumption > income : Poorer households report spending more than they earn - e.g. people can be drawing down savings, borrowing (students, retired people)
- Richer households earn more than they spend and save the rest.
- 
- What does this mean for inequality? inequality income > inequality consumption - e.g. World Bank researchers find income-based Ginis are about 13% higher than consumption-based ones on average.
- Mixing both can entangle a real difference with a measurement difference

[Figma node 37:147]

blocks.html:
PIP — consumption or income?
income inequality > consumption inequality

slides.notes:
- Usually, when a survey is done: whole pop -> households are sampled -> respond the survey 
- In this process, there are three main reasons why surveys have a blind spot at the top 
    - sampling: rich are few in number, so random sampling struggles to capture them
    - response: when they are sampled, many decline to take part
    - under-reporting: when they respond, they might underreport income, especially from investments and business ownership, the kinds more concentrated at the very top
- This is inherent to surveys and an argument for using other kinds of data - which is a key motivation for WID

slides.notes:
- We've just seen the problem with surveys: they struggle to see the richest - WID's starting point is that this is super important and that it matters a lot for inequality
- tax data because (for those that declare) it doesn't depend on participating in surveys - but that's a headache

- WID's approach is called Distributional National Accounts. It starts from the country's total income, as measured in the national accounts, and distribute it all of it out across the population.
- That total is bigger than what surveys measure, national income includes things that are not 'income'

Key issue: trying to distribute “national income” to individuals

slides.notes:
- and still disagreement even with such rich data 
- an famous example is the disagreement on the estimates of income inequality for the US, between Piketty, Saez, Zucman (WID team) and  Auten & Splinter 
- Both teams use the same underlying US data and aim to measure the same thing: how national income is distributed across individuals. But they disagree about whether (post-tax) inequality has risen in recent decades, and by how much. 
- One important reason for their different results is that they make different choices about how to allocate the large share (around 40% in recent years) of national income that doesn’t appear on individual tax data. 
- These assumptions matter a lot. On that, Deaton... 
- We got this chart from a post... highlighted there was also: 
Many of the choices made in earlier research by Piketty and Saez (2003), and later by PSZ, tended to push measured inequality higher. In contrast, almost all the choices AS have made tend to push top income share estimates down, relative to PSZ. Still, these decisions are not “just” political. There are key substantive issues at stake.

[Figma node 37:173]

blocks.html:
Even when there is rich data, there are disagreements
https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/measuring-income-inequality-primer-debate
Angus Deaton (2020) sums up the issue in this way:
 
“Allocating from tax returns is hard enough, because tax units are neither individuals nor households, but allocating the other half of national income is an immensely more difficult task, requiring assumptions that are rarely well supported by evidence and often seem arbitrary. Because distribution is such a controversial topic, these assumptions leave plenty of scope for politically-biased challenges, in which each commentator can choose their own alternatives and get almost any result they choose.”

- number of countries with rising, number of countries with falling - weighted average

[Figma spec] Bar chart of # countries (+ share of pop) with >= US in 2022, 1990 - ?; low opacity for countries where the survey is > 5 years away. # countries; Rising (> +2 points); Stable (2 points); Falling (> -2 points).

[Deck] The live chart (components/fig-high-inequality.js, data/scripts/38_high_inequality_panel.py): one column per year 1990-2024 for the 171 countries with a national PIP survey. Red = at least as unequal as the United States in 2022 in the same series and measure (US Gini 2022: PIP 0.413, PIP + WID top 1% 0.484, WID post-tax 0.461, WID pre-tax 0.587), navy = below; the light shade = the nearest survey is more than 5 years away (PIP series only). 'Rising / stable / falling' compares each year with a start year (default 2000): stable within +-2 Gini points, or +-5% for the top-10%, top-1% and Palma measures. Tabs switch series; the controls switch measure, view, start year, countries vs population share, and region.

How it differs from the World Bank's 'number of countries with high inequality' (June 2024 blog, Figure 2): the Bank uses a fixed Gini > 40 and 'the most recent survey at the time'. Only a two-sided nearest-survey match reproduces its own 2000 count (77; the strictly backward rule gives 59), so the chart uses the nearest survey either side, at any distance. On the Bank's own definition our PIP gives 73 in 2000 and 46 in 2022 (blog: 77 and 52; different PIP vintage). Caveats: old data dominate the early 1990s and the last years; a change resting on the same survey at both ends is zero by construction (the tooltip counts them); WID bars are always solid although most WID country-years are WID's own extrapolations; the 40 countries without a national survey are left out.
